passages.original: 24. De quibus etiamsi quidam Philosophi:p studentes scripserint, h ut Panætius, et lilius ejus apud Græcos, Tullius apud Latinos ; non alienum duxi a nostro munere, ut eliam ipse scrihrrem. Et sicut Tullius i ad erudiendum filium, ila ego quoque ad vos informandos filios meos; neque enim minus vos diligo quos in Evangelio genui, quam si conjugio suscepissem. Non enim vehementior est natura ad diligendum, quam gratia. Plus certe diligere debemus quos perpetuo nobiscum putamus futuros, quam quos in hoc tantum sæculo, lUi degeneres nascuntur .
passages.english: 24. Although certain philosophers, devoted to wisdom, have written about these things, such as Panaetius and his son among the Greeks, and Tully among the Latins, I did not consider it foreign to our office that I too should write [on them]. And just as Tully [wrote] to instruct his son, so I too [write] to form you, my sons; for I do not love you, whom I begot in the Gospel, less than if I had received you through marriage. For nature is not more powerful in loving than grace. Certainly we ought to love more those whom we believe will be with us forever than those [who are with us] only in this world. Those are born degenerate
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Philosophi:p studentes' read as 'philosophiae studentes' ('devoted to philosophy/wisdom'); 'lilius' as 'filius'; 'eliam' as 'etiam'; 'scrihrrem' as 'scriberem'; 'ila' as 'ita'; 'lUi' as 'Illi'. Stray letters h, i omitted as footnote marks. 'His son' (filius) of Panaetius is as the text reads; some editions may read differently. The last sentence continues into the following context ('often, such as disgrace their father').

passages.original: 43. Laudatur in a Platone , quod in Politia sua 11 posuit eum qui contra justitiam disputandi partes recepisset, postulare veniam dictorum quae noc probaret. et veri inveniendi atque examinandae disputationis gratia, illam sibi impositam personam dicere.
passages.english: 43. Plato is praised because in his Republic he represented the one who had taken up the part of arguing against justice as asking pardon for the things said which he did not approve, and as saying that this role had been imposed on him for the sake of finding the truth and examining the argument.
passages.notes: 'in a Platone' read as 'in Platone' (stray footnote mark); '11' omitted; 'noc' read as 'non'.

passages.original: 48. Quo decurso, proclive aestimo, ut refellam caetera. Et primo eorum assertionem, qui Deum putant curam mundi nequaquam habere, sicut c Aristoteles asserit usque ad lunam eus descendere providentiam. Et quis operator negligat operis sui curam? Quis deserat et destituat quod ipse condendum putavit? Si injuria est rpgere, nonne est major injuria fecisse;
passages.english: 48. With this completed, I think it easy to refute the rest. And first the assertion of those who think that God has no care of the world at all, as Aristotle asserts that his providence descends only as far as the moon. And what worker would neglect the care of his own work? Who would abandon and forsake what he himself thought fit to create? If it is a wrong to rule, is it not a greater wrong to have made;
passages.notes: 'eus' read as 'ejus'; 'rpgere' read as 'regere' ('to rule/govern'). Stray 'c' omitted. The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: 5U. Sed horum magistrum velut e ebriuin, et 15 Voluptatis patronum, ipsi qui putantur sobrii, irrident philosophi? Nam de Aristotelis opinione quid loquar, qui putat Deum suis contentum esse finibus, et praescripto regni modo degere, ut poetarum loquuntur fabulæ, qui mundum f inter tres ferunt esse divisum; ut alii coelum, alii mare, alii inferna coercenda imperio, sorte obvenerint : eosque cavere ne usurpata alienarum partium sollicitudine , inter se bellum excitent.
passages.english: 50. But do not the philosophers themselves, who are thought sober, mock the master of these men as a drunkard and a patron of pleasure? For what shall I say of the opinion of Aristotle, who thinks that God is content with his own bounds and lives within the prescribed limit of his kingdom, as the tales of the poets say, who relate that the world was divided among three, so that to some the heaven, to others the sea, to others the underworld fell by lot to be held under their rule; and that they take care not to stir up war among themselves by usurping concern for the others' portions.
passages.notes: '5U' read as '50'; 'e ebriuin' as 'ebrium'; stray '15', 'f' omitted. 'Master of these men' presumably Epicurus. The opening sentence is printed as a question; it may be rhetorical.

passages.original: 82. In omni autem servandum ætate, ut deceat quod agas et conveniat, et quadret sibi ordo vitae toæ. Unde c Tullius etiam ordinem putat in illo decore servari oportere : idque positum dicit in formositate , ordine, ornatu ad aciionem apto : quæ difficile ait loquendo explicari posse, et ideo salis esse intelligi.
passages.english: 82. But in every age it must be observed that what you do is fitting and suitable, and that the order of your life is consistent with itself. Hence Tully also thinks that order ought to be maintained in that seemliness, and says that it consists in beauty, order, and adornment suited to action; which, he says, can hardly be explained in words, and therefore it is enough that they be understood.
passages.notes: 'toæ' read as 'tuae'; 'aciionem' as 'actionem'; 'salis' as 'satis'; stray 'c' omitted.

passages.original: Quomodo enim sapiens qui non requirit auctorem suum, qui dicit lapidi : Pater meus es Iti (Jerem II, 27) : d qui dicit diabolo, ut Manichæus : Auctor meus es tu? Quomodo sapiens Arianus, qui mavult imperfectum auctorem habere atque degenerem, quam verum atque perfectum? e Quomodo sapiens Marcion atque Eunomius, qui malunt Deum malum quam bonum liaberc ? Quomodo sapiens, qui Deum suum non limet? Initium enim sapientiæ timor Domini (Psal. ex, 9). Et alibi habes : Sapientes non declinant de ore Domini, aed tractant 32 in confessionibus sui, (Prov.
passages.english: For how is he wise who does not seek out his Maker, who says to a stone, "You are my father" (Jer. 2:27), who says to the devil, as the Manichaean does, "You are my maker"? How is the Arian wise, who prefers to have an imperfect and degenerate maker rather than a true and perfect one? How are Marcion and Eunomius wise, who prefer to have an evil God rather than a good one? How is he wise who does not fear his God? For "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Ps. 110:10). And elsewhere you have: "The wise do not turn aside from the mouth of the Lord, but treat [of him] in their confessions" (Prov.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "Iti" read as "tu", "liaberc" as "habere", "limet" as "timet", "aed" as "sed". Stray letters "d" and "e" and the number "32" are treated as footnote marks and omitted. "Psal. ex, 9" is evidently Ps. 110 (Vulgate numbering); the verse cited is 110:10, and the edition's "9" is kept only in this note. "In confessionibus sui" is probably "suis". "Tractant" is taken as "discuss, treat of", with the object [of him] supplied. The Proverbs reference is completed in the following context (24:7).

passages.original: ł. Itaque philosophi e vitam beatam, alii in non dolendo posuerunt, ut Hieronymus : alii in rerum scientia, ut Heriilus, qui audiens ab Aristotele et Tbeopbrasto mirabiliter laudatam esse rerum scientiam , solam eam quasi summum bonum posuit ; cum illi eam quasi bonum, non quasi solum bonum laudaverint. Aliif voluptatem dixerunt, ut Epicurus : alii, ut Callipho, et post eum Diodorus, ita interpretati sunt, ut alter ad voluptatem, alter ad vacuitatem doloris, consortium honestatis adjungerent, quod sine ea non possit esse beata vita.
passages.english: Therefore, of the philosophers, some placed the happy life in freedom from pain, like Hieronymus; others in the knowledge of things, like Herillus, who, hearing that the knowledge of things had been wonderfully praised by Aristotle and Theophrastus, set it alone as the highest good, whereas they had praised it as a good, not as the only good. Others named pleasure, like Epicurus; others, like Callipho and after him Diodorus, interpreted it so that the one joined to pleasure, the other to freedom from pain, the partnership of the honourable, because without it there could not be a happy life.
passages.notes: Section number illegible ('ł'). 'Heriilus' read as 'Herillus', 'Tbeopbrasto' as 'Theophrasto'; stray 'e', 'f' omitted. Hieronymus is presumably Hieronymus of Rhodes.
